THE BACKFILL OR EXCAVATION OPERATIONS BEHIND THE BOX STRUCTURE SHALL BE MADE SIMULTANEOUSLY ON BOTH SIDES AND NO SIDE SHALL LAG THE OPPOSITE SIDE BY MORE THAN 1.0m HEIGHT OF SOIL. 12. THE CONTRACTOR SHALL MAINTAIN AN ACCURATE RECORD OF THE EXCAVATED MATERIAL INCLUDING NATURE OF SOIL AT FORMATION LEVEL AND GROUND WATER. THE RECORD FORMAT SHALL BE AGREED WITH THE ENGINEER PRIOR TO COMMENCEMENT. THE EXCAVATION RECORD SHALL BE REVIEWED AND APPROVED BY THE ENGINEER. Statement of Problem Urban infrastructures are becoming more complex last century. The importance of pipe detecting and the value of its application. Before excavation for maintenance of underground piping, it is necessary to understand the various site problems on topography and surface materials (e.g. position (depth and displacement) and size of other piping, as well as manholes); In order to prevent third party companies from possible damages to infrastructural equipments and people, severe damage will be generated from mistaken excavation of other piping. The severity might even affect the corporate image and living resources such as electricity, telecommunication and hydrology. Detection of underground pipeline and cable locations is very important, in addition, locations and positions of infrastructural elements with respect to each other must be known for the new infrastructural projects and for the process of operation and replacement of current infrastructure. 1.1. Introduction Developing Technologies are rapidly, so there are a lot of devices for the detection of pipeline and cable locations. These devices are working with two methods in general. One of them is electromagnetic detection method with electromagnetic induction, and the other is GPR (Ground Penetrating Radar) method working with the principle of determining the underground structure and underground holes. Especially with the new instruments and computer algorithms developed in the last years, the locations of infrastructural elements with respect to each other are determined more accurately. Ground penetrating radar (GPR) is a geophysical method that uses radar pulses to image the subsurface. This non-destructive method uses electromagnetic (EM) radiation in the microwave band (UHF/VHF frequencies) of the radio spectrum, and detects the reflected signals from subsurface structures. One of the most useful applications of GPR in urban infrastructural engineering is mapping and detection of buried pipes. This unique application becomes imperative due to the ever-growing urbanization in both developed and developing nations with its attendant demand for buried utilities. The construction, development and management of subsurface infrastructures has become a very viable business that attracts the attention of scientists and engineers over the past few years. Various utilities such as telecommunication and electric power cables, water and gas supply cables etc. are delivered through underground pipes of various sized buried at different depths. In many cases, maintenance of these infrastructures requires digging operation which leads to unintentional damage to some of the facilities. We fully expect you to align your team with their Service Responsibilities without delay and avoid mis-directing tasks within the Project Team. The Client reserves the right to claim for any losses either direct or indirect associated with the delay in respect of completing this review and assessment and the PMC shall consider this letter as notification of such. SULFATE RESISTING PORTLAND CEMENT (TYPE V) COMPLYING WITH BS 4027 SHALL BE USED IN ALL CONCRETE MIXES. 12. STEEL REINFORCEMENT SHALL BE GRADE 460 (BS 4449) STEEL BARS OR AS SPECIFIED. 13. ALL REINFORCEMENT IN MANHOLES/CHAMBERS SHALL BE EPOXY COATED AS SPECIFIED. 14. MINIMUM COVER TO REINFORCEMENT SHALL BE 50mm, UNLESS SPECIFIED OTHERWISE . 15. EXTERNAL CONCRETE SURFACES BELOW GROUND SHALL BE PROTECTED WITH BITUMINOUS WATERPROOF MEMBRANE 2.20mm AND PROTECTION BOARD 6.0mm AS SPECIFIED. 16. GRANOLITHIC CONCRETE SHALL BE FORMED IN ALL MANHOLE CHANNELS TO PROVIDE A SMOOTH TRANSITION OF SIZE AND GRADIENT FROM THE INLET(S) TO THE OUTLET STORM INVERTS. 17. ALL MANHOLES TO HAVE 3 COATS OF EPOXY PAINT PROTECTION LINING TO ALL EXPOSED INTERNAL CONCRETE SURFACES. 18. INTERNAL CEMENT MORTAR JOINTS OF STORM MANHOLE EXTENSION RINGS SHALL BE RAKED OUT AND ALL EXPOSED FACES SHALL BE LAMINATED WITH EPOXY PAINT. 19. ALL PIPES CONNECTED TO THE MANHOLES ARE TO BE PROVIDED WITH ADEQUATE PUDDLE FLANGES AS REQUIRED. 20. ALL STORM MANHOLES SHALL BE FITTED WITH HEAVY DUTY D400 DI COVERS TO BS EN 124. 21. GRANULAR BED AND SURROUND TO PIPES SHALL BE ENCLOSED IN GEOTEXTILE AS SPECIFIED FOR ALL PIPES. 22. ANY PIPELINE BELOW GROUND LEVEL ENTERING OR PROTRUDING FROM ANY STRUCTURE SHALL BE FITTED WITH TWO FLEXIBLE JOINTS ADJACENT TO THE STRUCTURE AS SPECIFIED UNLESS INDICATED OTHERWISE. 23. CONCRETE SURROUND SHALL BE PROVIDED TO STORMWATER PIPES WHERE THE COVER IS LESS THAN 1.2 METERS. 24. THE OIL INTERCEPTORS SHOWN IN THE DRAWINGS ARE OPTIONAL AND WILL BE USED IN CASE THERE IS NO OIL INTERCEPTOR LOCATED BEFORE THE POND IN THE WADI AREA. 25. excerpt: Case Report Review of AMCO (Asset Management Company) Interfaces with Infrastructure team and Inherent delays Role Stakeholder Authority within Diriyah with specific oversight on Asset Management AMCO specifically reviewing all elements of the project that will be managed by them following Handover. Traffic Management Traffic Lighting Streetlighting ICT / Security Structure Breakdown in Terms of Infra Package 1 – AMCO Review Team Pedestrian underpasses – shared with AMCO on 15th Jan 2025 Traffic Management – Shared with AMCO on 21st Feb 2025 ICT/Security – shared with AMCO on 6th Feb 2025 Drafted By Clive Walsh Assoc Project Director 26th March 2025 Package Submission Review Package 1 Submission Description Underpass Structure (BVD and UPASS 2) Submission Date 15.01.25 Issue Type E-mail Days Overdue (allowing 14 days) 60 days Package 2 Submission Description Traffic Management Submission Date 21.02.25 Days Overdue (allowing 14 days) 19 days Package 3 Submission Description ICT/Security Submission Date 06.02.25 Days Overdue (allowing 14 days) 34 days Current Permit Flow Assessment Marked Red below – Areas where the PMC Stakeholder management team should be monitoring and requesting escalation but not happening Permit Flow-Diagram Review Key Observations and Findings AMCO have raised queries on the packages which have not been effectively communicated. This needs more investigation noting comments from Traffic Management package were received on 6th February 2025 and returned on 18th March 2025 (32 days to respond from DC team) and there is no other evidence of comments issued on the other packages. We note in addition that there is no set defined ruling for receipt of submissions with some using ACX ie. ICT and others standard mail with external zip files. (Appendix 1.0) AMCO requested a form to be completed referencing “AM Purpose of Request” The form returned was– noting Land Handover form issued and email (Appendix 2) – noting this is the request form but really does not suit the purpose of what’s required 3.0 No direct authorized person from Infrastructure DG2 Package 1 team following up is evident due to the passage of time without any visibility. Nobody owns the issue. Falling between two stools ; Nawar and Joao both poorly failing to address the key issues and no record of sufficient escalation controls evident. 4.0 Unclear Submissions referencing correspondence below leads to delays in Package Understanding Lots of examples of unclear direction and confusion on both sides of the Issuing and Receiving scale. Clear Roles and Responsibilities needed on both sides. 5.0 Consistent and Poor reporting by PMC Stakeholder management team. Noticing there is only a reporting functionality with Engr Anas (AECOM) with the weekly stakeholder meeting and reporting but no visible escalation and monitoring of consistent delays. This could be very well as a result of continuous delays in absolutely everything and now the team is tired to expedite anything and changes are recommended. 6.0 On both visits to AMCO on 25th and 26th March we found both key persons references marked “*” were working from home and unavailable. Rayan Bakhit Commercial Asst Manager*Abdul Rouf Bandith Assoc Design Direction *Abdul Haman Al Amri Design Director Key

reason: The text describes a process for detecting and verifying underground utilities, which is a narrative report of procedures and findings.
excerpt: for Detection and Verification of Existing Underground Utilities The Purpose of this is to detection and verification of the underground utilitiesprior to commencement of any excavation works to ensure safety of the project operatives, personnel and the public; to avoid damages to buried utilities and assets. The process described in this can be summarized in the following : : Desktop utility record search includes the process of deification of the existing utilities within the survey area or the scope of work limits through the collation and analysis of existing as-built records. This should be carried out through the following process: Identify utility owners within the limit of works or survey area using the following source of information: Utility as-built drawings provided by the Client, PMC or the Engineer. BALADY Coordination certificate obtained by the Contractor. Refer to Appendix-1 for a sample of the coordination certificate. Note: Potential utility owners include SEC, NWC, Traffic police, Riyadh Municipality, DGCL AMCO, SWC, MODA, STC, Mobily, MEWA, etc. Upon identification of the affected utility owners, the Contractor will approach the identified utility owners to solicit up-to-date information and as-built drawings regarding the existing utilities. Deliverable of this step: The Contractor should collate the obtained as-built information and produce combined utility as-built records. The mentioned records to be composed of colored utility lines imposed on aerial images. Utility lines should indicate (as applicable) utility owner, type of utility, size, and depth (e.g. NWC; PW line, DI 300 mm, 1.5 m depth). Above records should be reviewed and approved by the CSC. Site reconnaissance shall compromise of a joint site visit by the Contractor and the CSC to validate the existing utility records obtained from step-1 and document the following: The presence of utility related surface features including manholes, inspection chambers, utility markers, feeder pillars, street lighting, traces of excavated trenches on paved roads, etc. Measurements between known surface features on the ground compared with those indicated in the utility records. Assessment of any conflicts between obtained utility records and actual site conditions. Deliverables of this step should include mark-up of the utility records along with supporting photographs. Detection: Detection involves the use of geophysical techniques to detect and locate the underground utilities within the survey area. Two techniques are generally applied to locate buried utilities: EML, Electro Magnetic Locating: Detection of buried utilities via a hand-held receiver using electromagnetic and radio frequency signals that are present in metallic utilities because of current flow or re-transmitted low frequency radio signals. GPR, Ground Penetrating Radar: The use of radar waves from a surface transmitter that can penetrate through ground materials and are reflected back to the instrument by a change of ground materials or other buried objects. The process of scanning utilities shall be as outlined below: Scanning device: The Contractor shall Submit technical data sheet, user manual, and calibration certificate for the CSC review / information. The Contractor to provide details of the device operator. Evidence of training provided either by the device manufacturer or amanufacturers’ s endorsed trainer has to be submitted to the CSC. A BACKDROP SHALL BE PROVIDED FOR PIPES 700 DIAMETER AND ABOVE. FOR SURFACE WATER SYSTEMS THAT INCLUDE GROUND WATER FLOWS, BACKDROPS SHALL BE PROVIDED. B1. WHERE THERE IS A DIFFERENCE IN LEVEL BETWEEN THE INVERT LEVEL OF INCOMING AND OUTGOING SEWERS THE FOLLOWING RULES APPLY: a) WHERE THE DIFFERENCE IN LEVEL IS LESS THAN 600 THE PIPE CONNECTION MAY BE DIRECT THROUGH THE MANHOLE OR GRADIENT ADJUSTED TO SUIT. DIRECT CONNECTIONS SHALL NOT DISCHARGE ONTO THE BENCHING. b) WHERE THE DIFFERENCE IN LEVEL IS GREATER THAN 600 AND LESS THAN 1200 A RAMP BACKDROP SHALL BE CONSTRUCTED c) WHERE THE DIFFERENCE IN LEVEL IS OVER 1200 AND LESS THAN 8000 A VERTICAL BACKDROP SHALL BE CONSTRUCTED. d) EXTERNAL BACKDROPS ARE PREFERRED. INTERNAL BACKDROP MAY BE USED WHERE EXTERNAL BACKDROP IS NOT POSSIBLE, SUBJECT TO THE APPROVAL OF THE ENGINEER. INTERNAL BACKDROPS SHALL BE MAXIMUM 300 DIAMETER AND SHALL BE FORMED IN DUCTILE IRON. DUCTILE IRON PIPES AND FITTINGS SHALL BE SUITABLE FOR 10 BAR (PFA) WITH EXTERNAL COATING. e) VORTEX DROP TO BE USED WHEN DIFFERENCE IN LEVEL IS GREATER THAN 8.0M. B2. WHERE INCOMING AND OUTGOING PIPE DIAMETERS DIFFER THEY SHALL BE SET SOFFIT LEVEL AND A TAPERED CHANNEL SHALL BE PROVIDED. NOTES APPLICABLE TO BACKDROP MANHOLES: 1. ALL DIMENSIONS ARE IN MILLIMETRES UNLESS OTHERWISE STATED. 2. ALL MATERIALS AND WORKMANSHIP SHALL BE IN ACCORDANCE WITH THE CURRENT Q.C.S. UNLESS OTHERWISE AGREED WITH THE ENGINEER. 3. WHERE THERE IS A DISCREPANCY BETWEEN THE REQUIREMENTS IN THE SPECIFICATION AND THOSE SHOWN ON THIS DRAWING THE SPECIFICATION TAKE PRECEDENCE. 4. VARIATION TO STANDARD DETAILS ARE PERMISSIBLE TO MEET SITE SPECIFIC REQUIREMENTS SUBJECT TO ENGINEER'S APPROVAL. 5. ALL JOINTS BETWEEN SECTIONS OF GRP LINERS SHALL BE LAMINATED OVER WITH 200mm WIDE RESIN RICH GLASS. 6. ALL JOINTS BETWEEN PIPES, FIXTURES AND GRP LINERS ARE SEALED. 7. ALL JOINTS BETWEEN CONCRETE SECTIONS ARE WATERTIGHT. 8. UNLESS DETAILED OTHERWISE, ALL INSITU CONCRETE SHALL BE GRADE SRC 40 AND ALL PRECAST CONCRETE SHALL BE GRADE SRC 50. 9. ALL INCOMING PIPES ARE LAID SOFFIT TO SOFFIT WITH THE OUTGOING PIPE UNLESS A RAMP/BACKDROP IS CONSTRUCTED OR AS SHOWN ON THE PLAN. 10.ROCKER PIPE IS 600mm IN LENGTH OR 1.5xD WHICH EVER IS GREATER. 11.GRP PIPES AND FABRICATIONS CAST INTO CONCRETE SHALL BE GRIT COATED. 12.ALL INTERNAL SURFACE EXCEPT GRP COVERED SURFACES ARE TO BE COATED WITH ONE COAT OF BITUMINOUS EMULSION AND TWO COATS OF BITUMEN PAINT. 13.REINFORCED MANHOLES SHALL HAVE A GRP LINER TO 300 ABOVE SOFFIT OF OUTLET PIPE. CHAMBER WALLS ABOVE THE LINER SHALL HAVE AN EPOXY PROTECTIVE COATING. 14.MANHOLES IN THE CARRIAGEWAY AND PAVED AREAS TO BE BACKFILLED FULL HEIGHT TO THE UNDERSIDE OF THE SUB BASE FROM THE EXCAVATED SURFACE TO THE MANHOLE WITH 4N/mm² FOAMED CONCRETE, MAXIMUM AGGREGATE SIZE 5mm. BUTTERFLY VALVES SHALL BE INSTALLED INSIDE CONCRETE CHAMBERS FOR PIPE DIA EQUAL TO AND MORE THAN Ø300. 4) IRRIGATION LINE SHALL BE INSTALLED WITH A SOIL COVER DEPTH OF 1.2m UNDER MAJOR ROADS AND 1.0m UNDER LOCAL ROADS. 5) THRUST BLOCK FOR HDPE PIPE SHALL COMPLY WITH SUPPLIER RECOMMENDATIONS, THRUST BLOCK WILL NOT BE REQUIRED FOR HDPE PIPE IF FUSION WELDED. CONCRETE THRUST BLOCKS SHALL BE PROVIDED FOR ALL OTHER PIPES AT ALL PIPE BENDS, TEES, REDUCERS AND INCASE OF CHANGE IN DIRECTION BOTH HORIZONTAL AND VERTICAL FOR DUCTILE IRON PIPES. 6) PIPES HAVING COVER LESS THAN 1.0m SHALL BE ENCASED IN PLAIN CONCRETE. 7) PRESSURE CAN BE REDUCED TO DESIRED LEVEL USING PRV AT PLOT CONNECTION (MAXIMUM 5 BAR) AND AT SOLENOID VALVE(MAXIMUM 7BAR). ALL PRV INSTALLATION SHALL FOLLOW THE ARRANGEMENT AS SHOWN IN STANDARD DETAILS DRAWING. 8) FOR EXACT LOCATION OF IRRIGAITON PIPE LINE REFER TO TYPICAL UTILITIES COORDINATION CROSS SECTIONS DRAWINGS. 9) INSTALL AIR / VACUUM RELIEF VALVES AT IRRIGATION MAIN LINE TERMINATION POINTS, OR TO HIGHEST POINTS AND FINAL LOCATION TO BE ADJUSTED SITE. 10) ALL PIPE DIAMETERS ARE NOMINAL PIPE SIZES, FOR HDPE, IT IS OUTSIDE AND FOR GRP, IT IS INSIDE. 11) CONTRACTOR SHALL COORDINATE THE LOCAL AUTHORITIES / MUNICIPALITIES TO OBTAIN THE CONSTRUCTION APPROVAL BEFORE CONSTRUCTION. 12) ALL EXISITNG UTILITIES SYSTEMS SHALL BE KEPT IN OPERATION UNTIL THE NEW SYSTEM IS PUT IN TO OPERATION, AND IN FULL COORDINAITON WITH CONCERNED AUTHORITIES. 13) THE IRRIGATION SYSTEM IS DISPLAYED DIAGRAMMATIC, AND THE CONTRACTOR MAY BE REQUIRED TO MAKE ADJUSTMENTS IN THE FIELD AT THE TIME OF INSTALLATION TO AVOID EXISTING OR PLANNED UTILITIES. THE CONTRACTOR, HOWEVER, IS ADVISED TO FOLLOW THE LAYOUT AS SHOWN ON THE PLAN AS MUCH AS POSSIBLE 14) INCASE OF CONFLICT OR DISCREPANCY BETWEEN THE INFORMATION SHOWN AND ACTUAL CONDITION ON SITE, CONTRACTOR SHALL PREPARE SHOP DRAWING AND SUBMIT TO THE ENGINEER FOR APPROVAL PRIOR TO COMMENCEMENT OF CONSTRUCTION. 15) FOR INTERFACE CONNECTION, CONTRACTOR SHALL BE RESPONSIBLE TO LOCATE THE EXISTING SOURCE (INTERFACE POINT) FOR THE PROJECT AREA AND MAKE CONNECTION WITH IRRIGATION MAIN SUPPLY SYSTEM. 16) THE CONTRACTOR SHALL COORDINATE WITH ALL RESPONSIBLE AUTHORITIES AND MINISTRIES REGARDING DATA OR LOCATION OF ALL EXISITNG UTILITIES AND REPORT TO THE ENGINEER. 17) THE CONTRACTOR WILL BE RESPONSIBLE FOR THE DISCONNECTION AND RECONNECTION OF THE EXISTING SERVICES TO THE NETWORK. 18) CONTRACTOR IS RESPONSIBLE TO VARIFY THE GROUND LEVELS. Each process is supplemented with tables documenting procedures, KPIs (where applicable), and SLAs (where applicable). All contents of this document are collaboratively developed with the Functional Process Owners and the Business Process Management Department. Process Review Cycle As the organization evolves, so does its operating requirements. Accordingly, these processes will continually evolve to meet DGDA’s requirements. There are two approaches used to update business processes: periodic reviews, and request based. Firstly, periodic reviews rely on reviewing the process on fixed time intervals (for example, quarterly, bi-annual, or yearly). This depends on business nature and requirements. Secondly, request based relies on process-owners or process users highlighting an issue with the designed process for improvement. All process changes will be reviewed internally by the BPM Team in conjunction with the Process Owner and Requestor to ensure an effective solution is developed and implemented. excerpt: Diriyah Gate II Development 48 4.5 Pre-Construction Survey Prior to the commencement of construction and demolition activities, a pre-construction survey must be undertaken to identify all environmental aspects such as the following (but not limited to): ▪ Air Quality: - Visual and PM10 monitoring at Project boundary points located near identified SRs; ▪ Noise and Vibration Levels: - Baseline conditions should be monitored one month before commencement of construction and demolition activities; ▪ Soil contamination. A visual or olfactory inspection should be undertaken for the following: - Inspection for any contamination and spillages; - Identification of land uses and activities with potential sources of contamination; - Discoloured soil and/or fibrous texture to the soil (e.g., asbestos). Odour can also indicate contamination with the release of noxious fumes; - Foreign objects present; - Previous soil workings; - Waste pits; ▪ Water and wastewater: - If dewatering is required, baseline groundwater monitoring (including groundwater levels and quality) shall be undertaken; ▪ Ecology: - A terrestrial ecology survey will be undertaken in the form of a site walkover around the Project area, work site areas, access roads and buildings; - Pre-construction monitoring should be undertaken to locate potential ecological assets that may require relocation / protection (e.g., native trees, lizard burrows, nesting birds and roosting bats); ▪ Archaeology / Cultural Heritage: - Surveys carried out by professional archaeologists; - Drone survey; - Demarcation of areas with potential archaeological significance; ▪ Traffic and Transport; - Baseline traffic and routes assessment is recommended for planning of routes; and, - Noise and vibration monitoring. Photographic evidence of baseline conditions shall form part of the pre-construction survey. 4.6 Environmental and Sustainability Monitoring and Reporting MOSTADAM for Communities and LEED for Cities are the preferred certification schemes to be pursued and will be adopted at various target levels and in various districts of DG II. excerpt: MEED Middle East business intelligence Contractors to start work in 2024 on Saudi Landbridge 21 NOVEMBER 2023 | BY YASIR IQBAL (/AUTHOR/YASIR-IQBAL) The project involves the construction of about 1,500km of new track and is one of Saudi Arabia's most anticipated infrastructure projects (https://www.linkedin.com/company/meed/posts/?feedView=all) Register for MEED's guest programme (https://guest.meed.com/register/) Saudi Arabia is preparing to start work on the $7bn Saudi Landbridge project early next year, as the negotiations for the final cost and financing of the project reach the closing stages. "After the official announcement by the National Industrial Development & Logistics Programme (NIDLP) on Tuesday, the project is expected to be live early next year," a source close to the project told MEED. In a report published by the local Arabic daily Aliqtisadia on Tuesday 21 November, Suleiman al-Mazrou, CEO of the NIDLP, said that the negotiations regarding the implementation of the project have reached advanced stages. Earlier this year, Transport & Logistics Minister Saleh al-Jasser said in a forum in Riyadh that Saudi authorities are undertaking negotiations (https://www.meed.com/saudi-arabia-in-final-landbridge-talks) with the Saudi China Landbridge Consortium (SLCC) to determine the final cost and financing of the project. The SLCC signed a memorandum of understanding to implement the project on a public-private partnership basis in October 2018. The SLCC was formed by Saudi Railway Company (SAR) and China Civil Engineering Construction Company. Al-Ayuni Contracting was named as the local partner for the consortium. Other members include French firms Systra and Thales; Canada’s WSP; Aldhabaan & Partners, the local partner of UK legal consultancy Eversheds & Sutherland; ALG Infrastructure; and Calx Consultancy. Landbridge lines The Saudi Landbridge project is one of the largest infrastructure projects planned in Saudi Arabia. The scheme is being implemented by the SAR. It comprises six lines. The first line involves the upgrade of the Jubail Industrial City internal network, which is currently under construction. It will require 10 kilometres (km) of track to be built. The second is the upgrade of the Jubail to Dammam railway line, which is also currently under construction. It will require 35km of track to be built. The third line involves the upgrade of the Dammam to Riyadh railway line, with 87km of track to be built. The fourth line, which is known as the Riyadh bypass, is from the existing network in the north of the city to the south. It is split into two packages, the first has 67km of track and the second has 35km. The fifth line is a link from Riyadh to Jeddah and then on to King Abdullah Port with three stations at Jamuma, Moya and Al-Doadmi. The Riyadh to Jeddah line will have 920km of track and the Jeddah to King Abdullah Port link will have 146km of track. THE SURVEY COORDINATE SYSTEM IS WGS84 - UTM 38 N AND LOCAL VERTICAL DATUM. 4. ALL DIMENSIONS SHALL BE VERIFIED ON SITE BEFORE PROCEEDING WITH THE WORK. 5. ALL DIMENSIONS SHOWN ON STANDARD DETAIL DRAWINGS ARE IN MILLIMETERS UNLESS OTHERWISE INDICATED. 6. THE CONTRACTOR HAS TO TAKE ALL NECESSARY PRECAUTIONS AND MEASURES TO DEAL WITH GROUNDWATER AND SURFACE WATER DURING CONSTRUCTION IN CASE WATER TABLE IS ENCOUNTERED. 7. THE CONTRACTOR SHALL VERIFY GROUND LEVELS BEFORE COMMENCEMENT OF WORK. 8. OIL INTERCEPTOR ARE PROPRIETARY ITEMS AND IT SHALL BE THE CONTRACTOR'S RESPONSIBILITY TO DESIGN AND CONSTRUCT AS PER MANUFACTURER'S STANDARDS AND RECOMMENDATIONS AND AS APPROVED BY THE EMPLOYER'S REPRESENTATIVE. 9. ANY DEVIATIONS FROM THE ALLOCATED CORRIDORS SHALL BE AGREED WITH THE EMPLOYER'S REPRESENTATIVE PRIOR TO CONSTRUCTION COMMENCEMENT. 10. COVER LEVEL OF MANHOLES/CHAMBERS SHOULD MATCH WITH SURROUNDING BITUMINOUS /PAVED AREAS. 11. ALL CONCRETE SHALL BE CLASS 'A' UNLESS OTHERWISE INDICATED. SULFATE RESISTING PORTLAND CEMENT (TYPE V) COMPLYING WITH BS 4027 SHALL BE USED IN ALL CONCRETE MIXES. 12. STEEL REINFORCEMENT SHALL BE GRADE 460 (BS 4449) STEEL BARS OR AS SPECIFIED. 13. ALL REINFORCEMENT IN MANHOLES/CHAMBERS SHALL BE EPOXY COATED AS SPECIFIED. 14. MINIMUM COVER TO REINFORCEMENT SHALL BE 50mm, UNLESS SPECIFIED OTHERWISE . 15. EXTERNAL CONCRETE SURFACES BELOW GROUND SHALL BE PROTECTED WITH BITUMINOUS WATERPROOF MEMBRANE 2.20mm AND PROTECTION BOARD 6.0mm AS SPECIFIED. 16. GRANOLITHIC CONCRETE SHALL BE FORMED IN ALL MANHOLE CHANNELS TO PROVIDE A SMOOTH TRANSITION OF SIZE AND GRADIENT FROM THE INLET(S) TO THE OUTLET STORM INVERTS. 17. ALL MANHOLES TO HAVE 3 COATS OF EPOXY PAINT PROTECTION LINING TO ALL EXPOSED INTERNAL CONCRETE SURFACES. 18. INTERNAL CEMENT MORTAR JOINTS OF STORM MANHOLE EXTENSION RINGS SHALL BE RAKED OUT AND ALL EXPOSED FACES SHALL BE LAMINATED WITH EPOXY PAINT. 19. ALL PIPES CONNECTED TO THE MANHOLES ARE TO BE PROVIDED WITH ADEQUATE PUDDLE FLANGES AS REQUIRED. 20. ALL STORM MANHOLES SHALL BE FITTED WITH HEAVY DUTY D400 DI COVERS TO BS EN 124. 21. GRANULAR BED AND SURROUND TO PIPES SHALL BE ENCLOSED IN GEOTEXTILE AS SPECIFIED FOR ALL PIPES. 22. ANY PIPELINE BELOW GROUND LEVEL ENTERING OR PROTRUDING FROM ANY STRUCTURE SHALL BE FITTED WITH TWO FLEXIBLE JOINTS ADJACENT TO THE STRUCTURE AS SPECIFIED UNLESS INDICATED OTHERWISE. 23. CONCRETE SURROUND SHALL BE PROVIDED TO STORMWATER PIPES WHERE THE COVER IS LESS THAN 1.2 METERS. 24. THE OIL INTERCEPTORS SHOWN IN THE DRAWINGS ARE OPTIONAL AND WILL BE USED IN CASE THERE IS NO OIL INTERCEPTOR LOCATED BEFORE THE POND IN THE WADI AREA. 25. INLET TYPE (EITHER CATCH BASIN OR KERB INLET) ARE INDICATIVE FOLLOWING THE DESIGN AND CORRIDORS. IN CASE CONTRACTOR FOUND ON SITE THAT TYPE OF INLET NEEDS TO BE CHANGED FOLLOWING THE ROAD AND SITE CONDITIONS , HE CAN PROCEED ACCORDINGLY. 26. HOUSE CONNECTIONS LOCATIONS ARE INDICATIVE AND TO BE CONFIRMED WITH PLOT OWNERS. 27. HOUSE CONNECTIONS OF PUMPSTATIONS TO BE CONNECTED TO THE OUTLET PIPES COMING FROM THE PUMP STATIONS

Where works are to be undertaken in areas containing existing services, the Contractor shall establish their precise location by hand-digging trenches or by other suitable means such as electronic scanning before laying any adjacent new service. The Contractor shall provide such information regarding existing services to the Engineer and shall include such details on his record and as-built drawings. The Contractor shall liaise with all service providers to confirm and identify all existing services information. In the event of unknown services being discovered during the carrying out of the Works, the Contractor shall immediately inform the Engineer in writing. Payment for diverting or sealing off and abandoning any of these services if necessary or working around the same will only be made where the proviso to (Information and Inspection) the Conditions of Contract applies and even then, only against certified records and subject to the prior authorization of the Engineer with the consent of the Employer. The Contractor shall locate dimensionally on its as-built drawings all services encountered on the Site. 7.5 Third Party Approvals and Notices The Contractor’s responsibility shall be to carry out and complete the whole of the Works to comply as a minimum with the requirements of each and every relevant statutory, regulatory and utilities authorities. Should the Contractor for any reason whatsoever cause such approvals, permits, consents, etc to be withdrawn, the Contractor shall be fully responsible for their reinstatement or re-issuance, irrespective of whether such were originally procured by the Employer. The Contractor shall not commence any element of the project including but not limited to; demolition, excavation, filling, construction or any other works until he has obtained written approval from the relevant statutory, regulatory and utilities authorities, and a copy of that approval has been submitted to the Engineer. The Contractor’s general obligations shall include, without limitation: a. obtaining the necessary approvals/ permits/ consents, etc for excavation works; b. the submission of the Contactor’s temporary works designs and shop drawings to the relevant authorities and Engineer, obtaining both approvals as applicable; c. complying with the relevant requirements of the Employer’s environmental commitments and any future requirements included within the updated environmental approvals with respect to the construction of the works; 189 of 216

Please be advised of the status and upcoming requirements regarding LAARs for material storage and excavated material as follows AICC has currently three approved material storage LAARs: LAAR-371, LAAR-364, and LAAR-306 However, LAAR-332, LAAR-136 and LAAR-269 are currently designated for hard rock dumping and crushing, with a portion allocated for 1a crushed material. After CSC assessment, the issue is not solely a lack of space, but rather Mismanagement of the existing designated areas. These areas must be utilized and organized more effectively to avoid congestion and disruption. In fact, the Engineer has issued a formal letter to AICC regarding poor LAAR management (Ref: IP-INF-054-0000-JCB-LTR-MN-000405-00) toward this subject. Excavated material required for backfilling must be planned and stockpiled in accordance with the approved infrastructure testing plan. This ensures availability at the correct stages and avoids unnecessary double handing. Taking into consideration the quantity required for sand bedding and padding, the quantity is purely supplied from a third party and can immediately supply to specific areas and it doesn’t require any storage area. The material not required for backfilling must be removed from the project site and disposed of in approved locations. Retaining excess or unnecessary material within the project boundaries and not aligned with the project sustainable plan is not acceptable However, Engineer/PMC/Client anticipates an increase in material storage requirements in September and due to the expiry of LAARs allocated to other contractors, The Contractor is requested to always and permanently to propose Laars and for other discipline to react immediately as we intend to request from SWL to allocate additional areas accordingly. This is a factor that is not happening and repeatedly highlighted by the Engineer on logistic meetings. AICC has requested additional LAARs for crushed material and proposed three new areas (DGII-LAAR-5.11, DGII-LAAR-23.1, DGII-LAAR-15.6 ) . However, SWL has rejected these proposals, as the areas are earmarked for upcoming construction by Asset. Following discussions with the Client, PMC, and the Engineer, AICC has been advised to submit alternative proposed areas for review. This matter was addressed in the logistics meetings held on 12-08-25 and 19-08-25 (find in attachment) Consequently, planning and management of material storage is essential to maintain site safety, progress, and compliance. We request that you submit a revised material management plan, clearly indicating how you will optimize available laydown areas, ensure alignment with the testing plan, and arrange timely removal of surplus material. In conclusion, effective planning and management of material storage is essential to maintain site safety, progress, and compliance. We kindly request that the contractors submit a revised material management plan, clearly indicating: Optimization of available laydown areas Alignment with the infrastructure testing plan Timely removal of surplus material Proposal of alternative Laar’s as per site conditions , Enc: N/A August 23, 2025 .: -054- Attn: Mr. ) [Recipient address] DG II – Infrastructure package I DD-2023-118 Response to Contractor Letter “Prevention Due to Inadequate Storage and Laydown Areas” Regards [Sender name][Sender position]

excerpt: Urban Planning & Municipal Affair - Permitting Process Manual Document Name: Building & Infrastructure Permitting Process Manual Approved Date: December 14, 2022 Document Owner: Urban Planning & Municipal Affair Version: 1.0 Document Prepared By: UMA/BPM iv Document Purpose This manual has been prepared to provide a detailed functional overview of Building & Infrastructure Permitting. The first section of the document provides an overview of the function and pertinent details. The second section provides detailed process maps developed in the BPMN 2.0 standard. Each process is supplemented with tables documenting procedures, KPIs (where applicable), and SLAs (where applicable). All contents of this document are collaboratively developed with the Functional Process Owners and the Business Process Management Department. Process Review Cycle As the organization evolves, so does its operating requirements. Accordingly, these processes will continually evolve to meet DGDA’s requirements. There are two approaches used to update business processes: periodic reviews, and request based. Firstly, periodic reviews rely on reviewing the process on fixed time intervals (for example, quarterly, bi-annual, or yearly). This depends on business nature and requirements. Secondly, request based relies on process-owners or process users highlighting an issue with the designed process for improvement. All process changes will be reviewed internally by the BPM Team in conjunction with the Process Owner and Requestor to ensure an effective solution is developed and implemented. Risk & Compliance Document Owner and the department staff shall ensure that the Risk and Compliance Management processes are integral part of their functional operations, embedded in the culture and should ensure compliance to activities stated within this document. The responsibility of any risk arising from these processes and reporting of any potential losses or actual incidents rests with the Document Owner / Process Owners. They should notify their respective Risk Champions to communicate this with Risk and Compliance Division and to update the risk register. If the document owner wishes or required to update this document, changes / amendments must be communicated to Risk and Compliance Division prior reflecting any change. Supplemental Documents This document needs to be read in conjunction with other governing documents developed in DGDA. For example, the Delegation of Authority (DOA), approved policy documents, committee charters, and other approved documents. These documents will be referred throughout this document as and when required. excerpt: Detailed Design Report Package 1 IP-INF-054-0000-JCB-RPT-DE-000013-A 29 Value Engineering 29.1 General As part of the DGII infrastructure design delivery process, value engineering study is an integral part of the design development process. The VE study process defines a sequence of activities that are undertaken during a VE study; before, during, and following a workshop. During the VE workshop, the VE team learns about the background issues, defines and classifies the project functions, identifies creative approaches to provide the functions, and then evaluates, develops, and presents the VE proposals to key decision makers. The VE methodology consists of seven sequential phases as depicted in Figure 29-1: below. Those are information, function analysis, evaluation, creative, develop recommendations, presentation, and finally implementation and follow-up. Each phase has its own purpose, objectives, and tasks. For example, the creative phase involves exploring the various ways to perform the function(s) identified in the function analysis phase. This allows team members to brainstorm alternatives to existing systems or methods that are in use. Brainstorming forces people to be creative and allows team members to speculate on all possible ideas to the problems presented, or alternatives to the function. Figure 29-1: Proposed Value Engineering Process for DGII Infrastructure Project Jacobs ideal proposition for DGII is to conduct VE workshop soon after completion of 60% preliminary design and cost estimates. Subsequently, the outcome of the VE workshop shall be implemented during the execution of the 60% preliminary design stage. Soon after completion of this stage and cost estimates are adjusted accordingly, a second round of VE workshop was conducted on 6th April 2023 for gauging the previous implementation and identifying plausible areas that could possibly be fine-tuned and implemented during the execution of the 90% preliminary design and for generating new VE ideas. Based on final VE session, VE initiative has been included in the Package 1 detailed design. 29.2 Value Engineering Basics by validating functionality and providing an equal or better solution without compromising the efficacy of the service or product. At present, the Value Methodology Basics followed by Jacobs for DGII VE exercise is as per SAVE International VE process. Value is defined as the ratio of function to cost and thus value can be increased by either improving the function or by reducing the cost. Value = Function / Cost The value engineering should be initiated as early as possible in the project life cycle. If value engineering becomes rework or causes project delays, it is no longer beneficial to the project. The below graph shows when value engineering moves from presenting a financial gain to a financial loss. The lower down the project cycle we implement value engineering, it may become counterproductive to the overall project budget. excerpt: Detailed Design Report_extract Package 1 - IP-INF-054-0000-JCB-RPT-DE-000013 [A] 24 January 2024 Potable Water and Firefighting (page 154 and next) “It shall be noted that the potable water alignment and design was based on the Masterplan of DGII 14.1.5 Rev08, further changes in the masterplan shall be considered in the upcoming submissions.” Introduction The concept of potable water system is to take main supply from National Water Company (NWC) water line 1200 mm (JF: or 1000mm as mention ahead?) located in King Khalid Road (KKR) (under construction) (JF: details of this project? Work programme coordinated with ours?) to supply the three proposed tanks in the development. Connection points: 2 in the north side of the development feeding Tank-1 and Tank-2 and 1 in the south side of KKR feeding Tank-3. The distribution system should include water connection to each building unit up to its boundary plot maintaining minimum pressure requirement as per NWC/MEWA standards. Individual plots developers shall be responsible for the design and construction of their internal potable water distribution systems. (Easting and Northing) shall be confirmed with NWC & DGCL. Design objectives and constraints Main objective of the hydraulic design is to achieve a minimum pressure requirement of 1.5 bar at all locations. The information about existing pressure at the source point in NWC network on the KKR road is not available yet, The design will be amended in the later stage’s once information about pressure at tie-in point and location is confirmed by the authority (JF: this is a major constrain and may lead to time and/or cost impact) Existing Potable Water Network The (existing) network is seen to be located along King Khalid Road (KKR), within Districts DE3, 5, 7, 8, and 11. Pipe diameters are varying in size from 110 mm to 1200 mm. Pipe material for the combined potable water/firefighting systems includes uPVC, Cast Iron (CI), Ductile Iron (DI) and Asbestos Cement (AC), Concrete Cylindrical Pipe (CCP). All existing AC pipes within the project boundary will have to be replaced and adequality removed according to health organizations standards. These include the 300 mm and 600 mm diameter pipelines along King Khalid Road. Discussion and coordination with NWC on these alternatives shall take place. (JF: work by which project? Infra? Demolitions?. Coordination required between AIC and third party/stakeholder) Design Basis and Criteria Three storage reservoirs will be provided with total storage as one-day average demand plus fire water requirement (893 m3 in each tank (31 L/S for 4 Hours at two Hydrants), as a minimum level of redundancy. The pumps design shall follow the Peak daily Demand plus Fire Fighting demand (PDD + FF) and to assure minimum pressure in the network at the plot connection = 1.5 bar and maximum pressure up to 5.0 bar. House connection Type: As per NWC standards, a water connection will be composed of a saddle connection mounted on a waterline, connection pipes, water meter boxes and other related and necessary items to complete the house connection assembly…. size shallaccommodate filling the plot storage tank in 8 hours as per the NFPA

THE CONTRACTOR IS RESPONSIBLE TO VERIFY THE GROUND LEVELS. THE TOP OF CHAMBERS/MANHOLES SHALL BE FLUSH WITH THE ASPHALT PAVEMENT OR WITH FINISHED SIDEWALK LEVELS IN PAVED STREETS AND IN UNPAVED AREAS AS SHOWN ON PLAN. 4. FOR CHAMBER/MANHOLE INTERNAL AND EXTERNAL WALLS PROTECTION REFER TO SPECIFICATION. 5. LOCATION OF MANHOLES, CHAMBERS AND ANCILLARY WORKS ARE INDICATIVE ONLY. EXACT LOCATION TO BE DETERMINED ON SITE BY THE CONTRACTOR IN CONJUNCTION WITH THE RELEVANT SERVICE AUTHORITY. 6. FOR PIPELINE BEDDING, MANHOLE/CHAMBER, DISCHARGE CHAMBER DETAILS REFER TO RELEVANT STANDARD INSTALLATION DRAWINGS. 7. SEWERAGE GRAVITY NETWORK PIPES ARE TO BE GLASS REINFORCED PLASTIC (GRP) FOR ALL PIPE SIZES UNLESS OTHERWISE STATED FROM NWC O&M DEPARTMENT IN ACCORDANCE WITH SPECIFICATIONS. 8. UNLESS INDICATED OTHERWISE SEWAGE RISING MAIN PIPES ARE TO BE DUCTILE IRON (DI). ALL IN ACCORDANCE WITH SPECIFICATIONS. 9. CONCRETE PROTECTION TO BE PROVIDED FOR PIPES HAVING COVER OF LESS THAN 1.50M 10. PROVIDE TWO FLEXIBLE JOINTS TO VALVE CHAMBERS/MANHOLES. PLACE FIRST JOINT AT A DISTANCE NOT MORE THAN ONE DIAMETER. PLACE THE SECOND JOINT AT A DISTANCE (X) NOT MORE THAN THE FOLLOWING. - FOR D < 450 MM, X = 2 PIPE DIAMTERES. - FOR D <450 <1000 MM, X = 1.20 M - FOR D > 1000 MM, X = 1.8M 11. COVERS OF MANHOLES AND CHAMBERS SHALL BE INSCRIBED WITH TYPE OF UTILITY, AUTHORITY HAVING JURISDICTION AND GRADE OF COVER IN BOTHE ENGLISH AND ARABIC. 12. DEPTH OF MANHOLES SHOWN IN BOQ SHALL BE MEASURED AS PER SPECIFICATIONS AND STANDARD METHOD OF MEASUREMENT OF MOWE. 13. BENCHING SLOPE IN MANHOLES SHOULD NOT EXCEED 10%. 14. USE CIRCULAR FRAME WITH ALL CHAMBERS/MANHOLES COVERS. 15. ALL CHAMBER/MANHOLE COVER SHALL BE HEAVY DUTY SUITABLE FOR HEAVY VEHICULAR TRAFFIC. 16. BACKDROP TO BE PROVIDED IF LEVEL DIFFERENCE BETWEEN INCOMING PIPE AND MANHOLE INVERT LEVEL IS MORE THAN 60CM (H > 60 CM) 17. MINIMUM OF 30CM CLEARANCE TO BE KEPT BETWEEN SEWER PIPE AND EXISTING OR FUTURE PLANNED SERVICES. 18. THE CONTRACTOR IS TO CO-ORDINATE WITH OTHER SERVICE LAYOUTS AND SUBMIT SHOP DRAWINGS INDICATING PIPE SIZES, LEVELS, GRADES AND PROFILES. 19. MINIMAL DEPTH OF THE INSPECTION CHAMBER TO BE 0.9M AS MEASURED FROM GROUND SURFACE TO THE INSPECTION CHAMBER INVERT. 20. HOUSE CONNECTION PIPE DIAMETER FOR PLOTS TO BE MINIMUM 150 MM INTERNAL OR MIN 160 MM OUTSIDE DIAMETER. 21. FOR DISCREPANCIES OR OMISSIONS IN THIS DRAWING CONTACT THE ENGINEER PRIOR TO CONSTRUCTION. 22. THE COPYRIGHT OF THIS DRAWING IS VESTED IN THE ENGINEER AND MUST NOT BE COPIED OR REPRODUCED WITHOUT WRITTEN CONSENT. 23. WHERE A MANHOLE IS SHOWN AT THE ROAD/KERB INTERFACE, THE MANHOLE COVER SHALL BE LOCATED SUCH THAT IT IS PLACED EITHER AT THE ROAD OR ON THE VERGE AND NOT TO BE LOCATED ACROSS THE INTERFACE. 24. IF THE CONTRACTOR EXPERIENCES DIFFICULTY IN LOCATING THE SERVICES, HE SHALL CONTACT THE RELEVANT SERVICE AUTHORITY FORASSISTANCE. ALL MANHOLES TO HAVE 3 COATS OF EPOXY PAINT PROTECTION LINING TO ALL EXPOSED INTERNAL CONCRETE SURFACES. 18. GRANULAR BED AND SURROUND TO PIPES SHALL BE ENCLOSED IN GEOTEXTILE AS SPECIFIED FOR ALL PIPES. 22. ANY PIPELINE BELOW GROUND LEVEL ENTERING OR PROTRUDING FROM ANY STRUCTURE SHALL BE FITTED WITH TWO FLEXIBLE JOINTS ADJACENT TO THE STRUCTURE AS SPECIFIED UNLESS INDICATED OTHERWISE. 23. ALJAZZAR g) ip ot I MOHAMMED OMAR JAZZAR CONSULTING ENGINEERS CO Auwsigl GILaiuS Ne ae dane AS yc 1. Statement of Problem Urban infrastructures are becoming more complex last century. The importance of pipe detecting and the value of its application. Before excavation for maintenance of underground piping, it is necessary to understand the various site problems on topography and surface materials (e.g. position (depth and displacement) and size of other piping, as well as manholes); In order to prevent third party companies from possible damages to infrastructural equipments and people, severe damage will be generated from mistaken excavation of other piping. The severity might even affect the corporate image and living resources such as electricity, telecommunication and hydrology. Detection of underground pipeline and cable locations is very important, in addition, locations and positions of infrastructural elements with respect to each other must be known for the new infrastructural projects and for the process of operation and replacement of current infrastructure. 1.1. Introduction Developing Technologies are rapidly, so there are a lot of devices for the detection of pipeline and cable locations. These devices are working with two methods in general. One of them is electromagnetic detection method with electromagnetic induction, and the other is GPR (Ground Penetrating Radar) method working with the principle of determining the underground structure and underground holes. Especially with the new instruments and computer algorithms developed in the last years, the locations of infrastructural elements with respect to each other are determined more accurately. Ground penetrating radar (GPR) is a geophysical method that uses radar pulses to image the subsurface. This non-destructive method uses electromagnetic (EM) radiation in the microwave band (UHF/VHF frequencies) of the radio spectrum, and detects the reflected signals from subsurface structures. One of the most useful applications of GPR in urban infrastructural engineering is mapping and detection of buried pipes. This unique application becomes imperative due to the ever-growing urbanization in both developed and developing nations with its attendant demand for buried utilities. The construction, development and management of subsurface infrastructures has become a very viable business that attracts the attention of scientists and engineers over the past few years. Various utilities such as telecommunication and electric power cables, water and gas supply cables etc. are delivered through underground pipes of various sized buried at different depths. In many cases, maintenance of these infrastructures requires digging operation which leads to unintentional damage to some of the facilities. Rates attach to specific **described items** under each classification — diameter, depth, material, condition — not to the classification code itself. excerpt: # PRC-501 — Design Reviews & Acceptance ## Scope PRC-501 governs the review and acceptance of design documents within the construction programme. It applies to all design submissions from consultants, architects, and engineers. ## Valid Design Review Statuses Only these statuses are permitted on design documents under PRC-501: - `FOR_COMMENT` — issued for review and feedback - `ACCEPTANCE` — accepted for use without further commentTANCE` — accepted for use without further comment - `BUY_OFF` — closed-out / agreed; no further iteration required - `PENDING_DEBRIEF` — awaiting formal debrief meeting - `SUPERSEDED` — replaced by a newer revision Plain-language equivalents permitted on the title block: `accepted`, `for comment`, `buy-off`. ## Forbidden Statuses on Design Documents These statuses are contractually prohibited on design documents and must never appear on design submissions:nts and must never appear on design submissions: - `APPROVED` - `APPROVAL` - `SIGN_OFF` ### Why APPROVED Is Forbidden The word `APPROVED` carries contractual liability. It implies that the reviewer has accepted the design and assumes responsibility for its content. PRC-501 explicitly prohibits this word on design documents to preserve the contractor's liability for design correctness. Use `accepted`, `for comment`, or `buy-off` instead. ### What This Means In Practicey-off` instead. ### What This Means In Practice - A QA officer who stamps a structural drawing `APPROVED` is non-compliant with PRC-501. The drawing must be re-stamped with one of the valid statuses. - A Lead Engineer cannot use `APPROVED` regardless of seniority — the prohibition applies to all signatories. - The same rule applies to `APPROVAL` and `SIGN_OFF`. ## Review Distribution Period ### Minimum Distribution Periodribution Period ### Minimum Distribution Period Design review packages must be distributed to relevant stakeholders at least **7 calendar days** before the scheduled Design Review Workshop. This is a minimum — anything shorter is non-compliant. The 7-day figure is **calendar days**, not business days. Weekends and public holidays count toward the period. ### Maximum Distribution Periodard the period. ### Maximum Distribution Period PRC-501 recommends a maximum distribution period of 14 calendar days. Distributing too far in advance encourages stakeholders to defer review and can dilute attention. ### Common Misconception The minimum review period is **not 30 days**. Some teams cite 30 days from other procedures or contract clauses; PRC-501 is explicit on 7 calendar days minimum. ### Worked Exampleon 7 calendar days minimum. ### Worked Example If the Design Review Workshop is scheduled for the 15th of the month, the review pack must be issued no later than the 8th of that month. Distributing on the 8th gives exactly 7 calendar days before the 15th. If the pack is distributed only 3 calendar days before the workshop, the workshop must be postponed by at least 4 additional calendar days to comply. ## Related Procedures - PRC-502 — Design Directives and Employer Approval - PRC-606 — Variation Orders vs Request for Modification (RFM) - PRC-402 — Non-Conformance Reports (NCR)

NOT a reproduction of the copyrighted FIDIC text — the official wording lives only in the published FIDIC booklet (© FIDIC 2019, all rights reserved).DIC booklet (© FIDIC 2019, all rights reserved). Sources: FIDIC (fidic.org) "The FIDIC Golden Principles", First Edition 2019 (paraphrased, mechanism-level); published legal/engineering commentary. Companion note: `fidic_contracts_red_white.md`. --- ## Why the Golden Principles exist FIDIC publishes balanced standard forms (the rainbow suite — see the Red/White note), but almost every real contract amends the **General Conditions** throughontract amends the **General Conditions** through **Particular Conditions**. FIDIC observed that heavily amended, one-sided Particular Conditions were distorting the fair risk balance to the point where a contract still *called* "FIDIC" no longer behaved like one. The Golden Principles (GPs) are the guard-rails. They define the essential character that must survive amendment. The test is simple:that must survive amendment. The test is simple: - A contract whose Particular Conditions **respect all five GPs** can properly be called a **FIDIC contract**. - A contract that **breaches any GP** is a distortion — it may still be legally binding, but it is **not a true FIDIC contract**, and the balanced-risk reasoning that FIDIC case law and commentary rely on no longer safely applies. They are drafting/audit principles, not contract clauses — you apply them when **writing or reviewing Particular Conditions**, not during day-to-day administration. --- ## The five Golden Principles (paraphrased)## The five Golden Principles (paraphrased) | GP | Principle (plain-language) | What it protects against | |---|---|---| | **GP1** | The duties, rights, obligations, roles and responsibilities of all the Contract Participants must stay **generally as set out in the General Conditions**, and suited to the project. | Re-writing the Engineer's / Contractor's / Employer's role until the standard mechanism no longer works. | | **GP2** | The Particular Conditions must be drafted **clearly and unambiguously**. | Vague, contradictory, or bolt-on wording that conflicts with the General Conditions and breeds disputes. | | **GP3** | The Particular Conditions must **not change the balance of risk / reward allocation** provided for in the General Conditions. | Shifting risk wholesale onto one party (usually the Contractor) — the most common and most damaging abuse. | | **GP4** | All **time periods** given to participants to perform their obligations must be of **reasonable duration**. | Unreasonably short notice/response windows engineered to trip a party into default or a time-bar. | | **GP5** | Unless the **governing law** forbids it, all formal disputes must go to a **DAB / DAAB** for a provisionally binding decision **as a condition precedent to arbitration**. | Deleting the dispute board so the only route is straight to costly arbitration/litigation. |--- ## How to apply them (review lens for Particular Conditions) When the platform reasons about a project's contract, the GPs are the checklist for

While the world was recovering from the global COVID-19 pandemic, countries progressively began to reopen their borders and resume regular trade, generating a booming market demand in many sectors including the construction industry. As a result, the industry has been severely affected by a combination of costs inflation, including transport cost, and unavailability or scarcity of construction inputs such as goods and labour. In addition to that, 2022 was impacted by the Russian invasion of Ukraine, and by differing COVID-19 policies in different countries, some of which continued to apply a strict zero-COVID policy throughout 2022 with total lockdowns. All the above resulted in severe disruption to the construction industry’s global supply chains. This Guidance Memorandum contains an outline of the provisions in FIDIC’s various general conditions of contract1 which can be relevant to help users deal with numerous scenarios which may arise in the above context. Readers should be aware that in 2020 FIDIC published a Guidance Memorandum dealing with the immediate consequences of COVID-19.2 That guidance remains relevant, and this paper will not repeat here the guidance given therein unless it is relevant to the issue under discussion. Readers should also have regard to the Contracts Guide3 published by FIDIC in relation to the clauses specifically referred to in this Guidance Memorandum. In line with its Golden Principles,4 FIDIC commends all members of the construction community to particularly keep in mind that FIDIC: • promotes cooperation and trust between contracting Parties; • does not support any Party taking undue advantage of its bargaining power; • discourages adversarial attitudes and encourages dispute avoidance; and • encourages timely and adequate payment in accordance with the Contract to maintain cashflow. excerpt: # Interior Finishes Take-off and Estimate — the Process Contract How interior quantities and resource costs are derived on this platform. This document states the PROCESS. It deliberately contains **no heights, no productivity figures, no rates**: those are project variables that change per project and even per floor, and they must come from the project's own documents, the project facts store, or the operator — never from a global default. ## The processr — never from a global default. ## The process 1. **Measure** — the drawing take-off gives, per floor: net room floor area, summed room perimeter, and room count (`drawing_qto`). 2. **Derive interior quantities** — `interior_finishes_takeoff` computes: - floor screed / floor tiling / ceiling finish areas = net floor area; - skirting length = perimeter − (doors × door width); - wall finish area = perimeter × floor-to-ceiling height − door area − window deductions;ling height − door area − window deductions; - blockwork element area = wall face area × shared-wall fraction (internal walls are shared between two rooms; the fraction is a declared modelling parameter). The calculator REFUSES when the height is missing — it names the variable to supply instead of assuming one. 3. **Split resources** — `resource_line_cost` computes, per line: labour = quantity ÷ daily output × trade day rate; plant = declared÷ daily output × trade day rate; plant = declared fraction of labour; material = quantity × material rate. Productivity and day rate are required inputs; a missing material rate is reported as NO SOURCED RATE, never as zero and never invented. 4. **Source the variables, per project** — in this order: - the project's own documents (sections and door schedules for heights and openings; priced bills for rates);ights and openings; priced bills for rates); - the project facts / memory store (values the operator confirmed for THIS project — heights per floor, agreed norms, market rates); - the curated knowledge base's published references (composite rates, trade day rates, material prices) — cited by source; - the operator, asked directly, when none of the above carries the value. 5. **Declare** — every deliverable restates the variables used and theirdeliverable restates the variables used and their source. An estimate whose basis section cannot name where each variable came from is not finished. ## Why no defaults A default height or norm silently wrong for one floor poisons every quantity derived from it, and the error is invisible because nothing asked for the value. A refusal that names the missing variable costs one question; a wrong hardwired fact costs a re-measure. The calculators therefore fail loudly on missing required variables, and agents ask.

Source: WBDG Operations & Maintenance, framed on ASHRAE Standard 202. Best-practice guidance, not a regulation — the project's O&M requirements and the client's facility-management procedures govern. Bridges the commissioning Systems Manual (see the commissioning note) to facility operations, and pairs with the BIM/COBie note for structured data handover. ## What O&M covers O&M is the full set of services that keep the built asset available and performing the function it was designed and built for — through its operating life, from handover onward. Source: WBDG Operations & Maintenance. ## Maintenance strategies## Maintenance strategies | Strategy | Basis | When it fits | |---|---|---| | Reactive (run-to-failure) | Fix on breakdown | Non-critical, cheap-to-replace items | | Preventive | Scheduled by time or usage | Most building systems; predictable wear | | Predictive (condition-based) | Monitored condition triggers action | High-value / critical equipment | | Reliability-centered (RCM) | Failure-mode analysis sets the strategy per asset | Complex, mission-critical facilities |Source: WBDG O&M practice (industry maintenance strategy hierarchy). ## The handover - Early involvement by the Commissioning Provider is critical so the Owner's Project Requirements (OPR), Basis of Design (BOD), Commissioning Plan, and the O&M Systems Manual develop together, not as an afterthought. - At substantial completion, after O&M training, the Owner assumes operational responsibility. Commissioning is not complete until off-season testing is doneis not complete until off-season testing is done and the systems manual is transferred to the Owner. Source: WBDG Building Commissioning / O&M handover. ## Systems / O&M Manual contents Per ASHRAE Standard 202-2018 and Guideline 1.4-2019, the Systems Manual includes: the OPR and BOD, submittals, as-built drawings, specifications, certifications, a Facility Guide (building operating parameters), operational and maintenanceperating parameters), operational and maintenance requirements and O&M manuals, training documents, and commissioning documentation (test/verification reports, final issue-resolution logs). Source: ASHRAE Standard 202-2018; Guideline 1.4-2019 (via WBDG). ## COBie handover COBie (Construction-Operations Building Information Exchange) is the structured delivery of asset information — equipment, spaces, spares, warranties — from theequipment, spaces, spares, warranties — from the construction team to facility management, in a spreadsheet/IFC form. It replaces hand-transcribing hundreds of pages of paper O&M manuals, so the FM system is populated from the project data directly. See the BIM reference note. Source: WBDG — Construction-Operations Building Information Exchange (COBie). ## How to use - Use this to explain O&M scope, maintenance strategy choice, the handover sequence, and what the Systems Manual / O&M Manual must contain. - The client's FM procedures and the project O&M specification are authoritative for a specific project — this is the general framework.

excerpt: # Design Objectives — The 8+1 Whole-Building Goals (WBDG) Reference guidance on the design objectives a high-performance building must balance. Source: WBDG Design Objectives. Best-practice guidance (how to think about a design), not a regulation or binding standard — the project brief and the client's requirements govern priorities. International practice, applies to KSA. These objectives are interdependent: a good design integrates them rather than optimising one in isolation. Grounds how the platform reasons about design trade-offs and brief/BOD analysis. ## The design objectives## The design objectives | Objective | What it means | |---|---| | Accessible | Usable by people of all abilities; accessible routes, entrances, and facilities (universal design). | | Aesthetics | The form, materials, and image of the building and its fit with context. | | Cost-Effective | Best value over the whole life cycle — life-cycle cost, not lowest first cost; value engineering. | | Functional / Operational | Meets the functional programme; systems integration, flexibility, durability, operability. | | Historic Preservation | Respects historic/existing fabric; adaptive reuse where relevant. | | Productive | Occupant comfort, health, and productivity — thermal comfort, lighting, acoustics, indoor air quality, ergonomics. | | Resilient | Resists and recovers from hazards and disruptions — robustness, redundancy, adaptability. | | Secure / Safe | Physical security, life safety, fire protection, and natural-hazard mitigation. | | Sustainable | Environmental performance — energy, water, materials, site, and indoor environmental quality (the home of LEED-type goals). |Source: WBDG Design Objectives. ## How they work together - The objectives are **interdependent** — decisions for one affect others (e.g. a sustainability move can improve productivity but change cost). A high-performance design evaluates and balances them, it does not maximise one alone. - **Cost-Effective** is judged on **whole-life cost** (life-cycle cost analysis), not first cost — durability, energy, and maintenance count.cost — durability, energy, and maintenance count. - **Sustainable** is where rating systems (e.g. LEED) live; WBDG frames the goal, the specific rating credits are a separate standard. ## How to use - Use this to explain what each objective covers and that they must be balanced. - The project brief / Owner's Project Requirements set the priority weighting for a specific project — this is the general framework. - When analysing a brief or basis of design, check which objectives are addressed and flag gaps (e.g. resilience or accessibility not mentioned) rather than inventing requirements.

Interpretation note: an SPI of 0.8 means the project has earned only 80 cents of value for every dollar planned. An SPI below 1.0 always means the project is behind schedule. ## CPI Traffic Light System The CPI Traffic Light is the standard executive-dashboard rule: - **GREEN — CPI > 1.00** — Under Budget, Cost Efficient. Keep doing what works. - **AMBER — 0.90 ≤ CPI ≤ 1.00** — Slightly Over Budget. Investigate and take action.lightly Over Budget. Investigate and take action. - **RED — CPI < 0.90** — Over Budget, Cost Inefficient. Take corrective action now. The RED threshold is **CPI < 0.90**. Anything below 0.90 is RED. The AMBER band is **0.90 ≤ CPI ≤ 1.00** (inclusive on both ends). A CPI of exactly 0.90 is AMBER. A CPI of exactly 1.00 is AMBER. The GREEN band is **CPI > 1.00** (strictly greater than 1.00). ### Worked Examplestrictly greater than 1.00). ### Worked Examples - CPI of 0.85 → RED (below the 0.90 threshold). - CPI of 0.91 → AMBER (above 0.90, within the 0.90-1.00 band). - CPI of 0.93 → AMBER. - CPI of 0.95 → AMBER. - CPI of 1.05 → GREEN (above 1.00). - CPI of 0.72 → RED. Box 71467 Dubai - UAE 20th January 201,8 Reference for Chadi Mahmoud To whom it may concern Dear Sirs, Chadi Mahmoud was recruited by Hill lnternational after an intensive screening process to identify best suitable candidate for the Construction Manager position on the Dubai Parks and Resorts Project. The project is the Middle East's largest integrated leisure and theme park destination located on Sheikh Zayed road in Dubai, United Arab Emirates. Spread over 25 million square feet, it features more than 100 rides and attractions, and consists of three theme parks: Motiongate Dubai, Bollywood Parks Dubai and Legoland Dubai, and one water park: Legoland Water Park. lt also encompasses Riverland Dubai, a themed retail and dining destination, as well as the Polynesian-themed family resort, Lapita Hotel. Chadi was assigned to my package The Riverland even though he is coming from EPC Oil and Gas environment he demonstrated great skills as Client Representative PMC managing various main contractors and consultants adopting a fast track multi-package strategy. Chadi is highly recommended for his technical expertise, he made the right decisions for day to day activities to meet the challenge and deliver the project on time with zero delay. ALJAZZAR g) ip ot I MOHAMMED OMAR JAZZAR CONSULTING ENGINEERS CO Auwsigl GILaiuS Ne ae dane AS yc 1. Statement of Problem Urban infrastructures are becoming more complex last century. The importance of pipe detecting and the value of its application. Before excavation for maintenance of underground piping, it is necessary to understand the various site problems on topography and surface materials (e.g. position (depth and displacement) and size of other piping, as well as manholes); In order to prevent third party companies from possible damages to infrastructural equipments and people, severe damage will be generated from mistaken excavation of other piping. The severity might even affect the corporate image and living resources such as electricity, telecommunication and hydrology. Detection of underground pipeline and cable locations is very important, in addition, locations and positions of infrastructural elements with respect to each other must be known for the new infrastructural projects and for the process of operation and replacement of current infrastructure. 1.1. Introduction Developing Technologies are rapidly, so there are a lot of devices for the detection of pipeline and cable locations. These devices are working with two methods in general. One of them is electromagnetic detection method with electromagnetic induction, and the other is GPR (Ground Penetrating Radar) method working with the principle of determining the underground structure and underground holes. Especially with the new instruments and computer algorithms developed in the last years, the locations of infrastructural elements with respect to each other are determined more accurately. Ground penetrating radar (GPR) is a geophysical method that uses radar pulses to image the subsurface. This non-destructive method uses electromagnetic (EM) radiation in the microwave band (UHF/VHF frequencies) of the radio spectrum, and detects the reflected signals from subsurface structures. One of the most useful applications of GPR in urban infrastructural engineering is mapping and detection of buried pipes. This unique application becomes imperative due to the ever-growing urbanization in both developed and developing nations with its attendant demand for buried utilities. The construction, development and management of subsurface infrastructures has become a very viable business that attracts the attention of scientists and engineers over the past few years. Various utilities such as telecommunication and electric power cables, water and gas supply cables etc. are delivered through underground pipes of various sized buried at different depths. In many cases, maintenance of these infrastructures requires digging operation which leads to unintentional damage to some of the facilities. excerpt: Request for Proposals Large-Scale AI Data Center Campus Development Partnership — Canada April 16, 2026 Introduction Anthropic invites qualified parties to submit proposals for the development of a large-scale AI data center campus in Canada. We are seeking partners with the geographic, political, financial, and subject-matter expertise to deliver a collective 1 GW of critical IT capacity (approximately 1.4 GW total utility load) within Canada by EOY 2028, with initial capacity operational by EOY 2027 and a preference for projects that scale further or deliver faster. This is an initial target that may increase, and we will consider a portfolio of smaller sites across several selected respondents where that optimizes for speed. The objective is to establish a secure campus in Canada that supports advanced AI workloads, contributes to Canadian economic development, adds net-new generation capacity and grid infrastructure, and advances Anthropic's mission. Consistent with Anthropic's published energy affordability commitments in the US, we intend to match our load with net-new generation, fund required grid upgrades, and avoid upward pressure on local electricity prices. A performance specification covering data center technical requirements is being made available to developers as Exhibit A. Respondents should review and address compatibility with those requirements in their proposals. Please note that our requirements diverge notably from a typical hyperscaler cloud data center: our SLA model is a two-tier mixed availability model enabling creative energy solutions; we demand higher rack densities and direct-liquid closed-loop cooling (with a baseline design requiring no make-up water for mechanical heat rejection); and we place a higher premium on speed-to-scale over efficiency/reliability. Respondents proposing a standard hyperscale reference product without addressing these deltas will be disadvantaged. Anthropic is briefing relevant federal and provincial government bodies on this RFP in advance of issuance, and is engaging directly with transmission system operators and regulated utilities in candidate provinces. Selection Framework Anthropic is selecting a long-term partner. We expect this RFP process may culminate in an award before all details of design and timing are fully defined. What is most important is that our development partners have the flexibility and comfort to operate in ambiguous and rapidly evolving requirements environments. We are prioritizing partners who demonstrate: - Control of a well-developed land bank and demonstrated ability to identify and transact on additional land parcels as required. - Deep expertise operating in Canada, with demonstrated ability to navigate land development, entitlement, and permitting processes in-province. - Expertise partnering with utilities and power developers (traditional and renewable) to deploy large-scale campus solutions. We are targeting a minimum 1.4 GW (total utility) campus. We understand there is limited Canadian precedent at this scale and will calibrate qualification criteria accordingly. - Demonstrated experience across the full data center delivery lifecycle: design, supply chain, construction, commissioning, and operations. - Financial and development capabilities aligned to a 1+ GW critical IT scale project. - Ability to meet our security requirements across development, design, and operations —internally or through an aligned third-party partnership. Statement of Problem Urban infrastructures are becoming more complex last century. The importance of pipe detecting and the value of its application. Before excavation for maintenance of underground piping, it is necessary to understand the various site problems on topography and surface materials (e.g. position (depth and displacement) and size of other piping, as well as manholes); In order to prevent third party companies from possible damages to infrastructural equipments and people, severe damage will be generated from mistaken excavation of other piping. The severity might even affect the corporate image and living resources such as electricity, telecommunication and hydrology. Detection of underground pipeline and cable locations is very important, in addition, locations and positions of infrastructural elements with respect to each other must be known for the new infrastructural projects and for the process of operation and replacement of current infrastructure. 1.1. Introduction Developing Technologies are rapidly, so there are a lot of devices for the detection of pipeline and cable locations. These devices are working with two methods in general. One of them is electromagnetic detection method with electromagnetic induction, and the other is GPR (Ground Penetrating Radar) method working with the principle of determining the underground structure and underground holes. Especially with the new instruments and computer algorithms developed in the last years, the locations of infrastructural elements with respect to each other are determined more accurately. Ground penetrating radar (GPR) is a geophysical method that uses radar pulses to image the subsurface. This non-destructive method uses electromagnetic (EM) radiation in the microwave band (UHF/VHF frequencies) of the radio spectrum, and detects the reflected signals from subsurface structures. One of the most useful applications of GPR in urban infrastructural engineering is mapping and detection of buried pipes. This unique application becomes imperative due to the ever-growing urbanization in both developed and developing nations with its attendant demand for buried utilities. The construction, development and management of subsurface infrastructures has become a very viable business that attracts the attention of scientists and engineers over the past few years. Various utilities such as telecommunication and electric power cables, water and gas supply cables etc. are delivered through underground pipes of various sized buried at different depths. In many cases, maintenance of these infrastructures requires digging operation which leads to unintentional damage to some of the facilities. excerpt: NON-CONFORMANCE REPORT (NCR) BÁO CÁO KHÔNG PHÙ HỢP Form No./Biểu mẫu số: QMS.C.3 GUIDANCE ON FORM USE An NCR can be initiated by any project team member upon observation. The observation is to be communicated to the PM/CS who will assess the observation and determine if an NCR is warranted, The PM/CS will complete part 1 of the NCR clearly detailing: - details of the observation - Variation from the specification / drawings - Identify if the NCR is related to a process or material/ product. (Analytics) The NCR will be issued to the Contractor responsible. The Contractor will review the NCR and issue a (1st) response within 3 days by completing Part 2 of the form. The response will include as a mimimun: - Details of proposed remedial action. - Calculations if required. - Brief / detailed Method statement for the remedial works. - details of specific materials to be used. DO not use MAR for this step. - Analytics - Declare: Replace, Repair, Use as is. - Analytics - 5 M root cause. - An NCR should be closed within 28days. If this is no achieveable the contractor should set a target date. The PM/CS will review that proposed rectifcation works. The PMCS may request a review by Design if considered appropriate. The PM/CS will return his review code to the Contractor using art 3 of the form. - Review Code A: Contractor can proceed with the recrification works. - Review Code B: The proposed rectification work are acceptable in principle but additonal information required. - Revoew Code C: Not approved. Contractor to look at alternative methods. The contractor will continue to submit/resubmit the proposed rectification works thought 2nd, 3rd, 4th .. response until Review Status A is received, Upon Receipt of Status A, the Contractor will execute the rectification works. Once the recification works are completed, the contractor will call for a works inspection (WIR) to have the works accepted. Once the WIR is accepted by the PMCS, The NCR will be closed and signed off by: - Contractor - PM/CS - MRH QAQC - MRH Rep. (PD/PM) The NCR Register will be updated accordling. NOTE: Technical Submittal Form and Material Approval Request forms are not requried for submitting attachments to the NCR. The NCR updates are the communication tool. All NCR communications and updates will be compiled to one NCR file on record. excerpt: # PRC-501 — Design Reviews & Acceptance ## Scope PRC-501 governs the review and acceptance of design documents within the construction programme. It applies to all design submissions from consultants, architects, and engineers. ## Valid Design Review Statuses Only these statuses are permitted on design documents under PRC-501: - `FOR_COMMENT` — issued for review and feedback - `ACCEPTANCE` — accepted for use without further commentANCE` — accepted for use without further comment - `BUY_OFF` — closed-out / agreed; no further iteration required - `PENDING_DEBRIEF` — awaiting formal debrief meeting - `SUPERSEDED` — replaced by a newer revision Plain-language equivalents permitted on the title block: `accepted`, `for comment`, `buy-off`. ## Forbidden Statuses on Design Documents These statuses are contractually prohibited on design documents and must never appear on design submissions: - `APPROVED`er appear on design submissions: - `APPROVED` - `APPROVAL` - `SIGN_OFF` ### Why APPROVED Is Forbidden The word `APPROVED` carries contractual liability. It implies that the reviewer has accepted the design and assumes responsibility for its content. PRC-501 explicitly prohibits this word on design documents to preserve the contractor's liability for design correctness. Use `accepted`, `for comment`, or `buy-off` instead. ### What This Means In Practicef` instead. ### What This Means In Practice - A QA officer who stamps a structural drawing `APPROVED` is non-compliant with PRC-501. The drawing must be re-stamped with one of the valid statuses. - A Lead Engineer cannot use `APPROVED` regardless of seniority — the prohibition applies to all signatories. - The same rule applies to `APPROVAL` and `SIGN_OFF`. ## Review Distribution Period ### Minimum Distribution Periodtion Period ### Minimum Distribution Period Design review packages must be distributed to relevant stakeholders at least **7 calendar days** before the scheduled Design Review Workshop. This is a minimum — anything shorter is non-compliant. The 7-day figure is **calendar days**, not business days. Weekends and public holidays count toward the period. ### Maximum Distribution Periodthe period. ### Maximum Distribution Period PRC-501 recommends a maximum distribution period of 14 calendar days. Distributing too far in advance encourages stakeholders to defer review and can dilute attention. ### Common Misconception The minimum review period is **not 30 days**. Some teams cite 30 days from other procedures or contract clauses; PRC-501 is explicit on 7 calendar days minimum. ### Worked Example7 calendar days minimum. ### Worked Example If the Design Review Workshop is scheduled for the 15th of the month, the review pack must be issued no later than the 8th of that month.
